newsitem.title: USA: Clinton appears to rule out Mideast arm-twisting.
newsitem.headline: Clinton appears to rule out Mideast arm-twisting.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday appeared to rule out U.S. arm-twisting to revive the Middle East peace process, saying it was up to Israel and the Palestinians to get stalled negotiations started again.

"I want these parties to do what they have to do to get this process up and going again. We've got to have an atmosphere of zero tolerance for terror but we've also got to have the kind of confidence-building necessary to make peace," Clinton said.

His comments to reporters at a meeting with Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien came as Israelis and Palestinians clashed anew one day after Clinton's apparently fruitless talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

In West Bank disturbances, Israeli soldiers and Jewish settlers shot two Palestinians to death and wounded 103, sparking angry demonstrations by hundreds of Palestinians who rained stones on Israeli soldiers guarding about 400 Jewish settlers in parts of Hebron still under Israeli occupation.

Clinton, under pressure from U.S. foreign policy experts and editorial writers to take a firmer stance in the growing crisis, said "the parties have got to do what it takes" to revive the peace process.

He called the latest outbreak of violence "troubling" but said it should not be allowed to divert attention from getting the negotiations going again because "that's the ultimate resolution of all these things."

Clinton repeated that he and Netanyahu had had "a long, thorough, very frank conversation" on Monday. "He's got some good ideas and I think we've got some good ideas and we want to talk to the Palestinians this week to see if we can get this going again," he said.
Earlier on Tuesday, the White House appealed for calm on the West Bank, saying violence erodes confidence in the value of negotiations.

"This is a time in which we are trying to build confidence between the parties and violence erodes confidence and reminds us all that ... restoring security is a principal aim of our effort, as well as a negotiating process that has integrity," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

Israeli-PLO peace moves have been frozen since March 18 when Netanyahu, defying international appeals, broke ground for new Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem. The construction, which Palestinians claim is designed to pre-empt negotiations on future control of that part of the city, ignited a wave of Palestinian demonstrations.
Netanyahu told an American Israel Public Affairs Committee dinner before his departure for home on Monday night his talks with Clinton were "excellent."
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Netanyahu agreed in meetings with Clinton and other U.S. officials to consider "specific American ideas," but he gave no details.

In remarks broadcast by Israel Radio, Netanyahu said Clinton "raised some suggestions for reviving the diplomatic process in a later stage ... I won't get into details but I can say the talk of pressures and threats and things like that did not come up at all."

Netanyahu's foreign policy adviser Dore Gold told CNN's "Crossfire" the two leaders reached a clear understanding that "for this process to go forward you can't have a link between bulldozers and dynamite ... between settlements and violence. Violence has to be removed from the process."

PLO official Hasan Rahman, on the same programme, rejected suggestions that Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat sanctioned the suicide bombing last month that killed three Israelis. "The first step is for Israel to stop building this illegal settlement and confiscating Palestinian land," he said.
